claims.text: High configurational entropy suppresses atomic diffusion in multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy suppresses phase separation in these nanoparticles.
Suppression of diffusion and phase separation maintains structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
A slight departure from an equiatomic composition reduces configurational entropy relative to a near-equiatomic composition.
Atomic-size mismatches among constituent elements cause lattice distortions.
High configurational entropy induces lattice strain.
Retarded atomic diffusion reduces elemental segregation.
Retarded atomic diffusion reduces nanoparticle coarsening.
Retarded atomic diffusion reduces phase separation.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles will preserve a uniform phase under high-temperature treatment better than slightly off-stoichiometric nanoparticles.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles will preserve compositional homogeneity under high-temperature treatment better than slightly off-stoichiometric nanoparticles.
Slightly off-stoichiometric nanoparticles will coarsen faster than near-equiatomic nanoparticles under otherwise identical high-temperature conditions.
Slightly off-stoichiometric nanoparticles will exhibit more elemental segregation than near-equiatomic nanoparticles under otherwise identical high-temperature conditions.
Slightly off-stoichiometric nanoparticles will exhibit more phase separation than near-equiatomic nanoparticles under otherwise identical high-temperature conditions.
The proposed entropy-mediated stability mechanism applies when constituent elements have moderate atomic-size disparities.
Extreme atomic-size disparities or large compositional deviations may activate alternative instability mechanisms.
